yes, a very bad idea. You'll be terribly slow because you have not developed any technique whatsoever. Every new note will look like something entirely new.

most people want just that: begin by some popular "song" they really like, but most probably even the easiest of these will be far beyond your beginner reach. Playing piano is not such torture.

You first must get yourself acquainted with the keyboard and develop a sense of your surroundings and evenness of tempo by playing scales with both hands - a major scale should suffice for a real beginner. True beginner pieces focus on the area around middle C and then progressively turn to the left hand on the bass clef and the right hand on the treble clef.

you could use this from a notorious 19th-century piano pedagogue as a guide:

http://imslp.org/wiki/Practical_Exercises_for_Beginners,_Op.599_(Czerny,_Carl)

be sure to play the very first pieces hands separate and then together when you got the rhythm right. Also note that in these very first exercises both right and left hands are playing in the treble clef in different areas: the left hand beginning in middle C and the right hand one octave above.

This work quickly steepens in difficulty by around the middle exercises. You could slow down a bit by trying also the excellent:

http://imslp.org/wiki/Les_Cinq_Doigts,_Op.777_(Czerny,_Carl)

This pedagogue is not just a repetitive warm-up: most pieces are short miniatures in early classical style. He is usually only disliked by advanced pianists required to learn his tough technical exercises, but the beginner stuff is pretty sweet. He was a pupil of a famous composer and teacher of another renowned pianist.
